Content:
To approximate the derivative of a function, we can use the finite difference formula

Content:
[MATH: f'(x)\approx \frac{f(x) - f(x-h) }{h}]
for small values of the step size [MATH: h,] with [MATH: h>0.]

Content:
This expression is known as the backward difference approximation because if [MATH: h>0] then [MATH: x-h] is a step behind [MATH: x] (i.e., to the left).

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/47c63598a080abcea1b31b02005e5d6b]

Content:
As usual, the smaller the step size [MATH: h] is, the better the approximation to [MATH: f'(x)] we obtain.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
We use the backward difference approximation formula [MATH: f'(x) \approx \frac{f(x) - f(x-h)}{h}]

at the point [MATH: x=16.] We choose the step size [MATH: h] to be as small as possible, in this case [MATH: h=3.] This gives

sections.normalized_html: The graph of the function [MATH: g(x)] is shown above. Approximate [MATH: g'(x)] at the point [MATH: x=6] using a backward difference approximation with step size [MATH: h=4.]

The graph of the function [MATH: g(x)] is shown above.
Approximate [MATH: g'(x)] at the point [MATH: x=6] using a backward difference approximation with step size [MATH: h=4.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
We use the backward difference approximation formula [MATH: g'(x) \approx \frac{g(x) - g(x-h)}{h},] at the point [MATH: x=6.] Applying the above formula with [MATH: x=6] and [MATH: h=4] gives

[MATH: g^{′}(6)|≈ (g(6) − g(6 − 4))/(4); = (g(6) − g(2))/(4); = (6 − 4)/(4); = (2)/(4); = (1)/(2).]

Approximate the marginal cost [MATH: C'(x)] at the point [MATH: x=3] using a backward difference approximation with step size [MATH: h=2.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
We use the backward difference approximation formula [MATH: C'(x) \approx \dfrac{C(x) - C(x-h)}{h},] at the point [MATH: x=3.] Applying the above formula with [MATH: x=3] and [MATH: h=2] gives

[MATH: C^{′}(3)|≈ (C(3) − C(3 − 2))/(2); = (C(3) − C(1))/(2); = (30 − 20)/(2); = (10)/(2); = 5.]

So the marginal cost is [MATH: \[math]5] per fan.

Where does the formula for the backward difference come from? Remember that from the definition of derivative, we have the forward difference formula
[MATH: f'(x)\approx \frac{f(x+h) - f(x) }{h}]
for small values of [MATH: h.]

Content:
Now, replacing [MATH: h] with [MATH: -h] in the formula above gives

Content:
[MATH: f^{′}(x)|≈ (f(x − h) − f(x))/(− h); = (f(x) − f(x − h))/(h).]

Content:
The step of replacing [MATH: h] with [MATH: -h] is equivalent to stepping a distance of [MATH: h] to the left rather than to the right.

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
To approximate the derivative of a function, we can use the finite difference formula

Content:
[MATH: f'(x)\approx \frac{f(x) - f(x-h) }{h}]
for small values of the step size [MATH: h,] with [MATH: h>0.]

Content:
This expression is known as the backward difference approximation because if [MATH: h>0] then [MATH: x-h] is a step behind [MATH: x] (i.e., to the left).

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/47c63598a080abcea1b31b02005e5d6b]

Content:
As usual, the smaller the step size [MATH: h] is, the better the approximation to [MATH: f'(x)] we obtain.

---

Item 2 — Example: Estimating a Derivative Given a Table Using a Backward Difference Approximation

Example Prompt:
A function [MATH: f(x)] has values according to the table below:

| [MATH: x] | [MATH: 1] | [MATH: 4] | [MATH: 7] | [MATH: 10] | [MATH: 13] | [MATH: 16] |
| [MATH: f(x)] | [MATH: -12] | [MATH: -7] | [MATH: -3] | [MATH: 7] | [MATH: 15] | [MATH: 21] |

Approximate [MATH: f'(x)] at the point [MATH: x=16] using a backward difference approximation.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We use the backward difference approximation formula
[MATH: f'(x) \approx \frac{f(x) - f(x-h)}{h}]

at the point [MATH: x=16.] We choose the step size [MATH: h] to be as small as possible, in this case [MATH: h=3.] This gives

[MATH: f^{′}(16)|≈ (f(16) − f(16 − 3))/(3); = (f(16) − f(13))/(3); = (21 − 15)/(3); = (6)/(3); = 2.]

---

Item 8 — Example: Estimating a Derivative Given a Table Using a Backward Difference Approximation: Word Problem

Example Prompt:
A race car's position along a straight track, measured in meters from the starting line, is given by the function [MATH: s(t),] where [MATH: t] is the time in seconds. The values of [MATH: s(t)] for different values of [MATH: t] are given in the table below.

| [MATH: t] | [MATH: 1.2] | [MATH: 1.4] | [MATH: 1.6] | [MATH: 1.8] | [MATH: 2.0] |
| [MATH: s(t)] | [MATH: 1.3] | [MATH: 2.7] | [MATH: 2.9] | [MATH: 3.5] | [MATH: 5.0] |

Approximate the velocity [MATH: s'(t)] when [MATH: t=1.6] using a backward difference approximation.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We use the backward difference approximation formula
[MATH: s'(t) \approx \frac{s(t) - s(t-h)}{h}]

at the time [MATH: t=1.6.] We choose the step size [MATH: h] to be as small as possible, in this case [MATH: h=0.2.] This gives

[MATH: s^{′}(1.6)|≈ (s(1.6) − s(1.6 − 0.2))/(0.2); = (s(1.6) − s(1.4))/(0.2); = (2.9 − 2.7)/(0.2); = (0.2)/(0.2); = 1.]

So at the time [MATH: t=1.6,] the velocity is approximately [MATH: 1\, \textrm{m}/\textrm{s}.]
